CausalChain: Subclonal DDR defects -> localized increase in somatic mutations -> neoantigen generation -> focal PD-L1 upregulation on tumor cells -> recruitment of immunosuppressive cells in the TME -> formation of an immune-excluded niche -> resistance to ICI monotherapy; Intervention with DDR inhibitors could further enhance neoantigen exposure and reduce immunosuppression -> improved ICI response.
Hypothesis: In biliary tract cancers, subclonal DDR deficiencies that do not cause overall MSI-high status elicit localized neoantigen production and focal PD-L1 overexpression, fostering an immune-excluded microenvironment. Targeting these DDR defects with specific inhibitors in combination with ICIs may convert these ‘cold’ regions into ‘hot’ immunogenic sites, thereby enhancing therapeutic responses.
Abstract: Despite the modest efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in biliary tract cancers (BTC), emerging evidence suggests that complex interactions among DNA damage repair (DDR) deficiencies, tumor mutational burden (TMB), and the tumor microenvironment (TME) may drive heterogeneous responses to immunotherapy. Here, we propose that subclonal DDR alterations, even in the absence of overt microsatellite instability, lead to localized neoantigen production that induces focal upregulation of PD‐L1 and paradoxically supports an immune‐excluded TME. This phenomenon may render certain BTC lesions refractory to ICI monotherapy while providing a window for synergistic combination strategies. We suggest that modulating the DDR pathway—potentially via selective DDR inhibitors—could augment neoantigen exposure and reshape the immune contexture, thereby enhancing sensitivity to ICIs. Further studies incorporating spatial mapping of DDR alterations and PD‐L1 expression are warranted to validate the clinical utility of targeting this axis in BTC.
